content:
Arthritis has different causes depending on the type. Osteoarthritis develops when joints cannot fully repair everyday wear and damage, with age, weight, injury and genes all playing a part. Inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, happens when the immune system attacks the joints. Gout is caused by crystals, and septic arthritis by infection. Often several factors combine.

Osteoarthritis: repair that cannot keep up

Joints are constantly repairing themselves. In osteoarthritis the balance tips: cartilage thins, the bone underneath thickens and bony growths form. Risk factors include:

  • age: most common after 45
  • being overweight: more load on knees and hips, and inflammatory chemicals from fat tissue
  • joint injury: such as a torn ligament or cartilage, or a fracture into a joint
  • repeated strain: jobs involving heavy lifting, kneeling or squatting
  • genes and family history, especially for hand osteoarthritis
  • being female, especially after menopause
  • joint shape: for example, hip problems from childhood
  • muscle weakness around the joint

Related reading: Gout: Causes, Symptoms and Treatment, Reactive Arthritis: Causes, Symptoms and Recovery, Inflammatory Arthritis: Types, Causes and Treatment (UK Guide)

Inflammatory arthritis: the immune system

In rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and lupus, the immune system mistakes healthy tissue for a threat. The exact trigger is often unknown, but contributing factors include:

  • genes, such as HLA-B27 in ankylosing spondylitis
  • smoking, the biggest lifestyle risk for rheumatoid arthritis
  • sex hormones, which may explain why RA and lupus are more common in women
  • having psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease
  • infections, which can trigger reactive arthritis

Crystal arthritis

Gout happens when uric acid builds up in the blood and forms needle-shaped crystals in joints. Risk factors include genes, kidney problems, being overweight, high blood pressure, drinking a lot of alcohol or sugary drinks, eating large amounts of red meat or seafood, and some medicines such as water tablets.

Pseudogout is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals and is more common in older people.

Infection

Septic arthritis is caused by bacteria getting into a joint, through the blood, a wound or after surgery. It is more likely in people with joint replacements, diabetes, weakened immune systems or existing arthritis. It needs emergency treatment.

What does not cause arthritis

  • cracking your knuckles: there is no good evidence it causes arthritis
  • cold or damp weather: may make joints feel worse but does not cause arthritis
  • normal exercise: helps keep joints healthy rather than wearing them out

Why understanding causes helps

Knowing what may have contributed to your arthritis can guide treatment. For example, weight loss helps knee osteoarthritis, stopping smoking helps rheumatoid arthritis and medicines that lower uric acid prevent gout attacks.

Risk factors you can change

  • keep to a healthy weight
  • stay active and keep your muscles strong
  • protect your joints at work and in sport
  • do not smoke
  • keep alcohol within recommended limits
  • get symptoms checked early

When to see your GP

See your GP if you have joint pain, swelling or stiffness that lasts more than a few weeks, stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes in the morning, or symptoms in several joints. Early diagnosis helps you get the right treatment.

A combination of factors

For most people, arthritis is not caused by a single thing. A person may inherit genes that raise their risk, injure a knee playing football in their twenties, gain weight in middle age and then develop knee osteoarthritis in their sixties. Similarly, rheumatoid arthritis may develop when someone with a genetic tendency smokes or has another trigger. This is why there is rarely one answer to the question "why me?", and why reducing the risks you can control is worthwhile.

It also means that arthritis is not your fault. Many of the factors involved are outside anyone's control, and what matters most now is getting the right diagnosis and support.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
